title: Contract Law Deep Dive: Formation Defenses, Interpretation & Remedies
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: A void contract is best described as one that:
options: Never had legal effect and cannot be ratified
Is valid until one party elects to rescind
Is valid but a court will not enforce it
rationales: Correct. A void contract never had legal effect and nothing can affirm it.
That describes a voidable contract.
That describes an unenforceable contract.
Attorney review is not what makes a contract void.

questions.stem: A contract induced by fraud is generally:
options: Voidable at the defrauded party's election
Unenforceable only under the Statute of Frauds
rationales: Fraud does not make a contract void from the start.
Correct. The defrauded party may elect to disaffirm or may instead affirm and sue for damages.
Rescission is not automatic; the injured party must elect it.
This is unrelated to the Statute of Frauds.

questions.stem: A seller tells a buyer a roof was 'fully replaced last year' when only a small section was patched, and the buyer relies on that statement and waives the roof inspection. This is most accurately described as:
rationales: Constructive fraud does not require an intentional false statement like this one.
Correct. An intentional material misrepresentation made to induce reliance is actual fraud.
Only one party was mistaken, and the seller knew the truth.
This is not about contract terms being one-sided.

questions.stem: Constructive fraud differs from actual fraud because constructive fraud:
options: Can arise from breach of a duty without intent to deceive
rationales: Intent is the element constructive fraud does not require.
Correct. It can arise from a breach of duty, such as a fiduciary's disclosure duty, even without intent to deceive.
It is actionable.
It is not limited to written contracts.

options: An unlawful threat overcoming free will
rationales: Ordinary hard bargaining is not duress.
Correct. Duress requires an unlawful threat that overcomes the will of the other party.
Appraisal outcomes are unrelated.
A missed deadline is unrelated to duress.

questions.stem: An isolated, dependent elderly seller is persuaded by a trusted relative to sell a home well below market value without independent advice. This fact pattern most strongly suggests:
rationales: Both parties did not share a mistaken belief here.
Correct. A position of trust combined with vulnerability and an unfair result is a classic undue-influence pattern.
Unconscionability is a separate, narrower doctrine focused on contract terms.
The parol evidence rule is unrelated.

questions.stem: A mutual mistake that can make a contract voidable involves:
options: Only one party being wrong about an unimportant detail
Both parties sharing an untrue belief about a material fact
A party changing their mind after signing
A party failing to read the contract
rationales: An unimportant, one-sided error does not qualify.
Correct. A shared, material misunderstanding of fact can make a contract voidable.
Buyer's remorse is not mistake.
Failing to read is not mistake in the legal sense.

questions.stem: A unilateral mistake generally excuses performance only when:
options: The other party knew or should have known of the error and tried to exploit it
The mistake involves the address only
The error is discovered after closing
rationales: Correct. A unilateral mistake typically excuses performance only if the other side knew or should have known and took advantage.
Regret alone does not excuse performance.
Address errors are not automatically excusing.
Timing after closing does not itself create the excuse.

options: Requires every contract to be notarized
Bars evidence of prior statements that contradict a final written agreement
rationales: Notarization is unrelated to this rule.
Correct. It bars evidence contradicting or adding to an integrated written agreement.
Later written modifications can still be shown; the rule targets prior/contemporaneous statements.
It is not limited to commercial leases.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller verbally agree the seller will leave the washer and dryer, but the written contract is silent. The safest professional practice is to:
options: Put the agreement in writing in the contract or an addendum
Wait until closing to mention it
rationales: Verbal side promises are difficult to enforce under the parol evidence rule.
Correct. Material terms should be written into the contract itself.
Nothing is automatically included without being written.
Waiting risks a dispute with no written basis.

questions.stem: A liquidated damages clause on a $650,000 purchase capped at 3% limits the seller's recovery, upon buyer default, to approximately:
rationales: That is 1%, not 3%.
That is 10%, not 3%.
That figure is far too high.

questions.stem: A liquidated damages clause will likely be struck down as unenforceable if it:
options: Operates as a penalty far exceeding likely harm
rationales: A reasonable estimate is enforceable.
Initials are a formality requirement, not a defect.
Correct. An amount so large it functions as a penalty risks being unenforceable.
Applying to buyer default alone is not itself a defect.

questions.stem: A seller who signs a valid purchase agreement then refuses to close because a better off-market offer appeared may face a buyer's remedy of:
options: Nothing, since sellers may always cancel
rationales: Correct. Because real property is unique, courts more readily order specific performance to compel the seller to convey.
Rescission is not automatic and does not fit this fact pattern.
A seller cannot lawfully cancel simply because a better offer appeared.
Liquidated damages against the buyer make no sense; the seller is the breaching party here.

questions.stem: Specific performance is more readily available in real estate contracts than for ordinary goods contracts because:
options: Real estate contracts are always written
Real property is considered legally unique
rationales: Being written is not the reason.
Correct. Land's legal uniqueness makes money damages an inadequate substitute.
Escrow does not require this remedy.
Buyer preference does not determine legal availability.

questions.stem: Rescission as a remedy is best described as:
options: Unwinding the contract to restore pre-contract positions
rationales: That describes specific performance.
Damages are a separate remedy.
Correct. Rescission restores both parties to their pre-contract position.
Rescission unwinds rather than modifies.

questions.stem: An adhesion contract is best described as:
options: A standardized, non-negotiable form offered by the stronger party
rationales: Adhesion contracts are routinely enforced.
Correct. It is a take-it-or-leave-it standardized form from the party with greater bargaining power.
Notarization is unrelated.
Adhesion contracts are typically written, standardized forms.

options: Only that one party had less bargaining power
Only that the contract was in writing
That the contract used standard association forms
rationales: Unequal bargaining power alone is not enough.
Being written is not the standard.
Correct. Courts typically require both procedural unfairness and substantively one-sided terms.
Using standard forms does not itself establish unconscionability.

questions.stem: When an agent suspects a contract dispute involves fraud, undue influence, or a formation defense, the correct professional step is to:
options: Resolve it personally to protect the deal
Draft custom contract language fixing the issue
Recognize the pattern, document facts, and refer to an attorney
Ignore it if the client does not raise it
rationales: Licensees may not practice law by resolving legal defenses.
Drafting custom legal remedies is practicing law.
Correct. Recognize, document, and refer — this is the boundary of the licensee's role.
Ignoring a recognized legal issue does not meet fiduciary or ethical obligations.
